docs.title: libbitcoin documentation
docs.text:
Documentation for the libbitcoin server stack: bs, the full node and query server, and the libraries it is built from.

  • Features

    What the server does: the protocols it speaks, the queries it answers, the modes it runs in.

  • Install

    Getting a binary: building from source, the build generator, packages, and docker.

  • Operation

    Running the node: store creation, sync, snapshots, the console, services, upgrading, and troubleshooting.

  • Configuration

    Every setting, its default, and what it controls. Command line, configuration file, and environment.

  • Interfaces

    The client-facing protocols, method by method: Electrum, bitcoind, btcd, ZeroMQ, and Stratum.

  • Test

    How the stack is tested, from a single method to a synced node on the public network.

  • Security

    Transport, authentication, isolation, and anonymity networks: what is exposed, to whom, and how.

  • Conformance

    Conformance to the interfaces it implements, method by method, with declared exceptions.

  • Performance

    Measured behavior: sync time, resource use, scaling with RAM and hardware, with the data behind each plot.

  • Architecture

    How the stack is built: the libraries, their boundaries, and the mechanisms that make the node fast.

  • Developer

    Building against the libraries: the public interfaces of each and how they compose.

  • Glossary

    The vocabulary used throughout the documentation and the code.

docs.title: Architecture
docs.text:
bs is one process built from five libraries. Each library is its own repository and depends only on the libraries below it.

flowchart TB
    server[libbitcoin-server]
    node[libbitcoin-node]
    network[libbitcoin-network]
    database[libbitcoin-database]
    system[libbitcoin-system]
    server --> node
    node --> network
    node --> database
    network --> system
    database --> system

docs.title: Libraries
docs.text:
libbitcoin-system is the foundation. It holds the chain types (block, header, transaction, script, witness), the script machine and its interpreter, hashing (SHA family, RIPEMD, SHA-3, SipHash, MuHash) with hardware intrinsics for Intel, NEON and SVE, and the wallet primitives (keys, addresses, mnemonics, descriptors, PSBT). Serialization, streams, endianness, radix encodings, unicode and configuration parsing live here too. Nothing in system knows about a network or a disk.

libbitcoin-database is the store. Tables are memory-mapped files built from three primitives: arraymap for positional records, hashmap for keyed records, and nomap for unkeyed bodies. The store owns the table set and the lifecycle operations create, open, snapshot, prune, restore, reload and close. The query class is the only interface the node and server use to read or write it.

libbitcoin-network is the connection layer. net owns the thread pool and a single strand, and runs sessions. A session maintains a set of channels. A channel is a proxy with timers and connection state, and a proxy is a serialized message pump over a socket. protocol objects attach to a channel and implement one message exchange each. Peer protocols are versioned by the protocol level that introduced them, so protocol_ping_60001 and protocol_version_70016 name their own history. The same machinery carries HTTP, JSON-RPC, TLS and ZMTP for client-server work, and SOCKS5 and I2P SAM for anonymity transports.

libbitcoin-node is the synchronizer. full_node derives from net, adds the store query, and composes ten chasers. Each chaser owns one stage of the pipeline and communicates with the others only through chase events. Node protocols extend the peer protocols with the block, header, transaction and filter exchanges that drive the chasers.

libbitcoin-server is the service layer. server_node derives from full_node and adds one session per client-facing service: admin, native, bitcoind, btcd, electrum, sparrow, esplora, stratum_v1, stratum_v2 and bitcoind_zmq. Each service session is a session_server parameterized by its protocol stack, so connection management, binding, and black and white listing are shared while parsing and serialization are per interface. The console directory holds the bs executable itself.

classDiagram
    direction TB
    class net {
        thread pool and strand
        peer sessions
        hosts pool
    }
    class full_node {
        store query
        ten chasers
        chase event bus
    }
    class server_node {
        ten service sessions
    }
    net <|-- full_node
    full_node <|-- server_node

docs.title: Process lifecycle
docs.text:
The bs executable is the console executor. Its run sequence is fixed:

flowchart LR
    A[open store] --> B[construct node] --> C[start] --> D[run] --> E[services] --> F[wait] --> G[close]

Store. If the store path exists it is opened. A flush.lock left by an unclean shutdown makes open fail and triggers restore from the most recent snapshot. If the path does not exist the store is created. Only then is the node constructed over the store's query.

Start. full_node::start starts every chaser, the header chaser or the block chaser according to headers_first, then check, validate, confirm, transaction, template, estimate, snapshot and storage. Control then passes to net::start, which starts the manual session, loads the hosts file, and runs the seed session to completion.

Run. full_node::run fires the chase::start event, which tells the chasers to begin from their current store positions. net::run connects the configured manual peers, then starts the inbound session, then the outbound session. server_node::run follows with the ten service sessions in order.

Stop. Close is idempotent and blocks until work has drained. The chasers are stopped, the event subscriber is stopped with chase::stop, the network closes its sessions and joins the thread pool, and finally the store is closed, which clears the flush lock.

From the network layer up the stack runs on the ASIO proactor. State belongs to a strand and changes only in handlers posted to it, so threads never wait on one another. Node and server contain no mutex at all, and network contains one, in a diagnostics capture. The store uses atomics and compare-and-swap for its hot paths and reserves exclusive locking for remapping a grown file. Concurrency covers the design in full.

docs.title: Event flow
docs.text:
Chasers do not call each other. Each subscribes to chase events and issues its own. The event names are the pipeline vocabulary:

Stage Events issued Issued by Candidate chain headers, blocks, regressed, disorganized header, block, organize Download download, starved, split, stall, purge check, block_in protocol Check checked, unchecked, windowed block_in protocol, check Validate valid, unvalid validate Confirm confirmable, unconfirmable, organized, reorganized, block, stale confirm Mining transaction, template_ transaction, template Control start, bump, suspend, resume, space, unfull, snap, report, stop full_node, organize, storage, executor; snap has no issuer today

Failures flow back to organize, which reorganizes the candidate chain away from the offending block and re-issues bump so the downstream chasers restart from their new positions.

docs.title: Concurrency
docs.text:
The rule across the stack is that a thread never blocks waiting for another thread to release shared state. State has one owner, a strand, and is read or changed only by handlers running on that strand. Where a primitive does appear it guards a rare structural event, such as growing a file, and never a hot path.

Node and server declare no mutex. Network declares one, in a diagnostics capture buffer. The store's few guard structural events described below. Strands, by contrast, are everywhere: stranded() asserts guard several hundred method entries across network, node and server.

docs.title: The proactor
docs.text:
network::threadpool owns one boost::asio::io_context and a set of threads that run it. Every socket operation, timer and posted handler completes on one of those threads. Nothing blocks on I/O. A read is issued and the thread moves on. When bytes arrive, the completion handler is dispatched to whichever thread is free.

Ordering comes from strands. A boost::asio::strand is an executor that guarantees its handlers never run concurrently, without pinning them to a thread. The pattern throughout the stack is: an object owns a strand, its mutable state is touched only from handlers on that strand, and any method callable from outside posts to the strand rather than acting directly. The POST macro does this for a member function, BIND produces the bound handler, and PARALLEL posts to the pool without a strand for work that is independent.

docs.title: Ownership by strand
docs.text:
net has one strand for cross-object state: session attachment, suspend and resume, subscriptions. Its stranded() returns true only on that strand, and start, run and close assert it.

Sockets post every handler except accept to an internal strand. Proxies and therefore channels run all completion and event handlers on the channel strand. A channel's protocols share that strand, so a protocol's handle_ methods are always stranded and a protocol never needs a lock of its own. A protocol is thread safe in the documented sense that its public methods either post to the strand or are called during handshake before concurrency exists.

Sessions are thread safe by the same construction. Each maintains a channel set on the net strand.

Chasers each own a strand on the network pool. A chaser's handle_chase runs on the strand of the notifier that fired it, so a chaser that needs its own state posts to itself with POST and returns. Chasers never call one another. The validate chaser additionally owns a second thread pool and strand, sized by the threads setting and scheduled at the configured priority, so block validation cannot starve network handling.

Service sessions in the server derive from the same session and channel machinery and inherit its strands. The server adds no synchronization primitive.

docs.title: Lifetime without locks
docs.text:
Handlers outlive the calls that create them, so object lifetime is managed by the handlers themselves. BIND_SHARED binds a member function to a shared_ptr obtained from shared_from_base, keeping the object alive until the handler runs. BIND_WEAK binds through a weak_ptr and the handler becomes a no-op if the object has gone. Channels warn that a pointer should only be retained while subscribed to the channel's stop, and released in the stop handler, otherwise the channel leaks.

Stop is a message, not a lock. Every proxy, session and chaser exposes an idempotent stop that posts to its strand, and subscribers to stop are invoked there with error::service_stopped. net::close is the one blocking call in the stack. It is documented as not callable from a pool thread, because it joins the pool.

docs.title: Joining without locks
docs.text:
Three families of handler combinators replace condition variables and barriers.

Subscribers. subscriber, desubscriber and unsubscriber hold handlers in a queue or keyed map. All methods must be invoked on the owning strand and handlers are invoked there. notify invokes each in order, stop invokes each with a code and drops them. A desubscriber's handler returns whether to remain subscribed. The chase event bus, connect and close notification, and every channel's stop subscription are built on these.

Races. A race joins N asynchronous completions into one. race_all completes on the last finisher. race_any completes on the first. race_speed<N> completes with the first result once all N have finished, and is what the validate chaser uses to complete a block with its first error. race_quality completes on the first success, used by outbound sessions to keep the first handshake that succeeds. race_unity completes on the first failure once all have finished, used by the seed session to continue once enough seeding has occurred. race_volume completes when a count is reached. All but race_any are documented not thread safe because they run on a strand.

Turnstiles. The validate chaser batches signatures across blocks. Batch state lives in the store rather than in memory, in the ecdsa, schnorr and prevalid tables, so the batch is crash-durable and any completing pool thread can service it without coordination. The drain and commit exclusion is a turnstile: entering capture and exiting capture are counted so that a commit waits for in-flight captures to leave, without blocking any writer from entering.

docs.title: The store
docs.text:
The store is fully concurrent for writers against writers and for readers against writers. Neither takes a lock on the request path. This rests on three facts: bodies are append only, an element becomes reachable only after it is complete, and the publication that makes it reachable is a single atomic word store with release semantics.

Allocation. A writer claims rows by advancing the body's logical_ extent with a compare-and-swap. Two writers never receive the same rows, and neither waits for the other. The memory map maintains a chain of extents, settled_ <= frontier_ <= logical_ <= capacity_ <= file_, in which the lower bounds move on the lock-free fast path and the upper bounds move only under the remap lock, so a stale-low read of a lower bound can never falsify the chain.

Publication. A hash table head is a memory-mapped array of bucket cells. A cell holds the link of the newest element in the bucket in its low bits and a small bloom filter over the keys in that bucket in the rest. Its width is set per table by the schema. To commit an element, the writer writes the element's body and its next link, which is the bucket's current top, then issues a release fence, then replaces the cell by compare-and-swap with the new link and the updated filter. The fence orders the element's bytes before the word that exposes them, so a reader that observes the new cell observes a complete element and a complete chain. Contention between two writers on one bucket costs one retry of the swap. A reader loads the cell with acquire semantics, screens the key against the filter, and walks the chain by following next links, none of which change once published. This is the path for a cell of native word width. A cell of another width cannot be swapped atomically, so that head falls back to a shared mutex, exclusive for the update and shared for the read. The positional height indexes store links with relaxed atomics, since their ordering comes from the reorganization interlock below.

Remap. The one exclusive event is growing a body past its capacity, because it can move the mapping. An accessor into a body holds a shared remap lock for its lifetime and remap takes the exclusive lock. So the primitives insist that an iterator, reader or finalizer be used for serialization and disposed immediately, and that no accessor into one table be held while reading the same table or another. A remap waiting on that accessor while the accessor waits on a read of the same table is a deadlock. The hashmap.get(iterator, ...) overload exists so a read can complete through an accessor already held. Memory commitment follows use in chunks within a standing disk reservation, so growth is a syscall per chunk and not a remap.

Interlocks. Two shared mutexes in query order candidate and confirmed reorganization against concurrent readers of those indexes. The store transactor is a shared lock taken by query holders for the duration of an operation, with snapshot, prune and close taking the exclusive side. Close waits in one-second attempts until readers have drained. These guard chain-level events measured in seconds, not element writes measured in nanoseconds.

docs.title: What this buys
docs.text: There is no lock ordering to reason about, because there are no nested locks in the request path. A slow peer cannot stall another, because their channels are on different strands and a proxy's write queue is per channel. A slow disk cannot stall the network, because validation runs on its own pool and the network pool's handlers are short. A crash cannot corrupt the store's in-flight state, because the state that matters, including the signature batch, is written through to the store as it is produced.

docs.title: Network layer
docs.text:
libbitcoin-network is a general asynchronous connection layer. The peer-to-peer protocol is one client of it. HTTP, JSON-RPC, WebSocket, TLS, ZMTP and the BIP-324 encrypted transport are the others, and every service the server exposes is built on the same session, channel and protocol classes as a peer connection.

flowchart TB
    net
    subgraph sessions
        manual
        seed
        inbound
        outbound
        server
    end
    net --> sessions
    sessions -->|attach| channel
    channel -->|attach| protocols
    channel --> proxy --> socket

docs.title: net
docs.text:
net owns the threadpool, the strand on which cross-object state changes, and the hosts address pool. It runs sessions. start starts the manual session, loads the hosts file, and runs the seed session to completion. run connects the configured manual peers, then starts the inbound session, then the outbound session. close stops everything and joins the pool. suspend and resume stop and restart peer connections without touching service connections, which are managed independently.

net also publishes two subscriptions: subscribe_connect, invoked for each channel created, and subscribe_close, invoked on service stop. Disconnection has no subscription of its own. A subscriber to connect subscribes to each channel's stop instead.

docs.title: Sessions
docs.text:
A session maintains a set of channels and is thread safe by construction, since it works on the net strand. The four peer sessions differ in how they obtain connections:

  • manual maintains a connection to each configured peer, reconnecting on loss, with a callback per attempt.
  • seed connects to the configured seeds, collects addresses into the hosts pool, and completes once enough seeding has occurred, joined by a race_unity.
  • inbound accepts connections on the configured binds up to the inbound connection limit, subject to black and white lists and the loopback guard.
  • outbound takes random addresses from the hosts pool and races several connection attempts, keeping the first handshake that succeeds by race_quality.

session_server is the client-server variant. It is documented as nearly identical to session_inbound, differing in handshake and protocol attachment, and it does not derive from session_peer so that downstream services do not inherit peer semantics.

docs.title: Channels, proxies and sockets
docs.text:
A socket wraps an ASIO TCP socket, or one of its TLS, BIP-324 or ZMTP variants, and posts all handlers except accept to an internal strand.

A proxy is a serialized message pump over a socket. It owns the read loop and a write queue. Full-duplex writes are queued to prevent interleaving, and the completion of one write starts the next. Sends are rate limited by allocating each bytes / rate_limit of time and deferring completion by whatever the write did not consume, which throttles the channel without a second queue. Reads are not metered, because they are bounded by protocol correctness. When a channel stops with pending writes the queue is purged and the purged handlers are not invoked.

A channel is a proxy with timers and connection state: expiration, inactivity, creation and last activity times, a nonce for the loopback guard, and an identifier for session subscribers. Protocols are attached to a channel with attach<protocol>() and started by the caller, on the strand. A channel also holds the dispatch gate. A protocol that needs to defer the next read until its dispatch completes, such as a query that reads the store, holds the gate and releases it when done, and the read is re-armed on release.

Connections are made by connector and acceptor, each with a variant: connector_socks for outbound through a SOCKS5 proxy such as Tor, and acceptor_sam for inbound forwarded by an I2P SAM bridge. Both are stranded and expose an idempotent thread safe stop.

docs.title: Protocols
docs.text:
A protocol implements one message exchange and nothing else. It subscribes to the messages it handles, its handle_ methods run on the channel strand, and it can stop its channel but never its session or the network. Protocol start has no failure condition.

Peer protocols are named by the protocol level that introduced their behavior, and the name is the history: protocol_version_106, protocol_version_70001, protocol_version_70002, protocol_version_70016; protocol_ping_106, protocol_ping_60001; protocol_address_in_209 and protocol_address_in_70016 with their _out counterparts; protocol_seed_209 and protocol_seed_70016; protocol_alert_311; protocol_reject_70002. The node adds the block, header, transaction and filter exchanges in the same style, from protocol_block_in_106 through protocol_transaction_in_70013 and protocol_filter_out_70015.

Selection is two-staged. At handshake, session_peer attaches the highest version protocol the configured protocol_maximum allows: 70016 if BIP-155 is configured and enable_address_v2 is set, else 70002 if BIP-61 and enable_reject, else 70001 if BIP-37, else 106. After the handshake, protocols are attached according to what was negotiated with the peer: ping with nonce if BIP-31, the plain ping otherwise; address v2 if BIP-155, else the original address exchange; alert and reject only if negotiated and enabled. A declined protocol is handled by registering its negotiation message and subscribing nothing, so an unknown command is never silently ignored.

docs.title: Messages
docs.text: Peer messages live under messages/peer, one class per message with a common heading. Serialization goes through a registry so a channel deserializes only messages a protocol has subscribed to. HTTP requests and responses, JSON bodies, and RPC framing live beside them and are used by the server's service protocols.

docs.title: Transports
docs.text:
• BIP-324 is the p2ps socket variant. The session cipher generates an ephemeral keypair, exchanges ElligatorSwift-encoded public keys in the clear, and derives the directional packet ciphers, garbage terminators and session identifier from the shared secret. Decoy packets are detected and dropped. It is selected per outbound address by the privacy flag.
  • TLS wraps a socket in an ASIO SSL context configured from tls_server settings: key, certificate, certificate authority, and passphrase.
  • ZMTP implements the CurveZMQ mechanism over ZMTP framing, with NaCl boxes for the handshake commands and messages, used by the bitcoind_zmq notification service.
  • HTTP and WebSocket are protocols, not sockets. protocol_http subscribes to requests by verb, dispatches to virtual methods, and answers disallowed verbs and invalid requests with standard responses. A WebSocket upgrade is accepted by the proxy on request.

docs.title: Hosts
docs.text: The hosts pool is a thread safe address table loaded from and saved to a line-oriented text file at the configured path. Duplicates and invalid addresses are discarded. Outbound sessions take one random connectable address of a requested family, and the pool reserves addresses currently connected so they are not taken twice. Counts by family are available for administration.

docs.title: Node pipeline
docs.text:
full_node composes ten chasers. A chaser owns one stage of chain construction, runs on its own strand, and communicates with the other chasers only through chase events on the node's shared notifier. Chasers impose order where order is required and nowhere else. Unlike protocols, a chaser can stop the node.

Chaser Owns header Chases stronger header branches for the candidate chain. Weak branches are retained in a hash table if not stored. A strong branch reorganizes the candidate chain and fires headers. block The blocks-first counterpart to header, organizing whole blocks and firing blocks. check Maintains the set of pending download identifiers for the candidate header chain and hands them to peers. validate Chases blocks in the candidate header chain for validation, on its own thread pool. confirm Chases valid blocks for confirmation and maintains the confirmed chain index. transaction Chases unconfirmed transactions: validates submitted packages and maintains the pool. template Constructs template blocks upon modification of the transaction DAG. estimate Maintains a running fee estimate cache over confirmed blocks. snapshot Prunes the prevout cache once the chain has coalesced, and takes a snapshot on snap. storage Monitors capacity following a disk full condition and restarts the network when space returns.

header and block are two instantiations of one organize template. Which one starts is decided by the headers_first setting. The rest of the pipeline is the same in both modes.

flowchart LR
    peers((peers))
    organize
    check
    dl[block_in]
    validate
    confirm
    out[out protocols]
    snapshot
    transaction
    template
    peers -->|headers, blocks| organize
    organize -->|headers / blocks| check
    check -->|download| dl
    dl -->|checked| validate
    check -->|windowed| validate
    validate -->|valid| confirm
    confirm -->|organized, stale| out
    confirm -->|block| snapshot
    confirm -->|organized, reorganized, block| transaction
    transaction -->|transaction| template
    dl -.->|unchecked| organize
    validate -.->|unvalid| organize
    confirm -.->|unconfirmable| organize
    organize -->|regressed, disorganized, bump| check
    organize -->|regressed, disorganized, bump| validate
    organize -->|regressed, disorganized, bump| confirm

organize is the header chaser or the block chaser. block_in is the download protocol on each peer channel. out protocols are the header, block and transaction announcers and the fee estimator. Solid arrows are forward progress. Dashed arrows are failures, and every failure routes to organize, which is the only chaser that changes the candidate chain.

docs.title: Organize
docs.text:
A header or block arrives from a peer protocol and is posted to the organize chaser. The sequence for each:

  1. Skip existing and orphan. A duplicate returns its stored state. A header whose parent is unknown is an orphan and is dropped.
  2. Validate the parent and obtain chain state. A parent already marked unconfirmable short-circuits, so a failed block cannot be looped over. A fork at or under the top reached checkpoint is rejected as a checkpoint conflict. Parent state comes from the cached top state, the header tree, or the store, in that order.
  3. Roll chain state forward from the archived parent to the new header, giving the context in which the header is checked and accepted.
  4. Validate and check currency. Header check and accept are never bypassed. Block bodies are validated later by the validate chaser, so malleation is ignored until then.
  5. Compute relative work. A header extending a weak branch is cached in the header tree and nothing else happens. Weak branches are held until the branch is strong enough to matter.
  6. Reorganize the candidate chain when the branch is stronger. The candidate chain is popped down to the branch point, the tree headers of the strong branch are archived and pushed, and the new header becomes the candidate top. The milestone flag is computed from the tree here because it trickles down, and is archived in the header record.
  7. Reset top state and notify. headers or blocks fires from the branch point once the chain is current, delayed at startup so headers can get current before block downloads start. regressed fires when the reorganization branched below the previous top. The top reached checkpoint advances and the tree is purged at and below it.

Reorganization following an unconfirmable block, disorganize, walks the same path in reverse: the candidates above the invalid block are moved out of the index, the strongest known alternative branch is reevaluated, and disorganized fires so the downstream chasers reset.

prioritize is bitcoind's preciousblock: a manual tie break between equal-work branches. Only the top of a cached branch can tie the candidate top. The preference is not retained.

docs.title: Check and download
docs.text:
The check chaser tracks two frontiers over the candidate chain. requested is the last height in the current download window. advanced is requested less the blocks not yet validated. Peers do not decide what to download. A block_in protocol asks the chaser for a set of hashes with get_hashes, downloads them, and returns any it did not complete with put_hashes, otherwise the chain would remain gapped.

The window is sized from the connection count. Each peer request is limited to the protocol's maximum inventory, and the window step is that maximum multiplied by the number of connections, capped by maximum_concurrency. Each block_in protocol reports its download speed to the chaser through the performer base. The chaser keeps the speeds of all channels and, once there are enough to measure, reports a channel whose speed falls below the others by more than allowed_deviation standard deviations. That channel splits its work, returning half its hashes for a faster peer, and stops. A stalled channel is dropped outright. stall splits every channel with work, and purge drops all outstanding work, both used when the window has to move.

Each downloaded block is checked for identity before storage: the block hash, the merkle root, and the witness commitment. Under checkpoint or milestone that is all that is required, and a block failing it is stored as invalid so it is never downloaded again. Pruned nodes do not store input scripts or witnesses under bypass at all. Check, accept and connect are deferred to the validate chaser, because requiring only identity here permits the simplified block_view type. The protocol fires checked for each block and the chaser fires windowed when a full window completes.

docs.title: Validate
docs.text:
The validate chaser walks the candidate chain by height from its last valid position. For each checked block it posts a validation job to its own pool with PARALLEL, so blocks validate concurrently up to the configured threads.

A job populates the block's previous outputs from the store, then runs check, accept and connect in the block's chain context. Under milestone or checkpoint the script evaluation is bypassed and the block is marked valid on identity alone, which is the source of the milestone sync speed. Above the milestone everything runs.

Signature verification is batched. Captured ECDSA and Schnorr signatures are written into the ecdsa and schnorr tables as rows, and the prevalid table carries each block's link set, so the batch is store-resident and crash-durable. Any completing pool thread may drain the batch. When a batch verifies, every block in it is marked valid at once and valid fires for each. A failure marks the block invalid and unvalid fires, routing to organize. Capturing is disabled once the confirmed chain is current and the node is not under bypass, so at the top of the chain signatures verify directly.

docs.title: Confirm
docs.text:
The confirm chaser follows valid by height. A block becomes confirmable when every input spends an output that is strong at that height, with no double spend. The strong_tx index records which transactions are strong in which block, and it is what confirmation consults. A confirmable block is pushed to the confirmed index and organized fires with its link. When the block's branch replaces a previously confirmed one, the popped blocks are rolled back and reorganized fires for each. An unconfirmable block fires unconfirmable, routing to organize.

Once the confirmed chain is current, each new confirmation also fires block, which the transaction and snapshot chasers act on, and starts a stale timer. If no block arrives within the timer, stale fires so the transaction protocols know the chain is no longer current.

docs.title: Snapshot, storage and the pool
docs.text:
The snapshot chaser prunes the prevout cache once, on the first confirmed block after the candidate and confirmed chains have coalesced, since the cache exists to serve validation of blocks that are now behind the confirmed top. It also handles snap by taking a snapshot, though nothing in the node issues that event today, so snapshots are operator driven through the console. Snapshots and prunes suspend the network for their duration and resume it afterward.

The storage chaser wakes on space, which the node fires when a disk full condition is detected, and polls the store's required space on a timer. When enough has been freed it reloads the store and fires unfull, which the validate chaser uses to resume.

The transaction chaser accepts submitted packages as a whole. A package is validated in the current pool context and archived unless submitted as a test, in which case nothing is stored. Each organized or reorganized block recomputes the pool context, and if the chain is found to be no longer current the pool is closed until it is. transaction fires for each accepted transaction, and the template chaser rebuilds the block template on it. The estimate chaser populates a fee accumulator from confirmed blocks up to fee_estimate_horizon and resets if the chain falls far behind.

docs.title: Store
docs.text: libbitcoin-database is a set of memory-mapped tables and one query class over them. There is no database engine, no write-ahead log and no page cache of its own. The operating system's virtual memory is the cache, a table is a file, and a link is an offset into it.

docs.title: Layout on disk
docs.text:
<path>/
  heads/                 one head file per table
  archive_header         one body file per table
  archive_tx
  ...
  primary/               most recent snapshot of heads/
  secondary/             previous snapshot, rotated
  temporary/             snapshot in progress
  flush                  held while the store is loaded
  process                held while a process has the store open

Every table is a head and a body. The body holds the records, append only. The head holds the table's bucket array for a hash table, or just the record count for a positional one. Body files sit at the store root, named archive_, index_, cache_, batch_ or option_ by their group. Head files sit under heads/.

Snapshot rotates directories atomically. temporary/ is emptied, primary/ is renamed to secondary/, the heads are dumped to temporary/, and temporary/ is renamed to primary/. The rotated secondary/ is then deleted on a best-effort basis, because the snapshot is committed once primary/ exists. Restore reverses this: an invalid heads/ is cleared and primary/ is cloned into it, or secondary/ if primary/ is missing, and the body files are truncated to the sizes recorded in the restored heads. A store that is flush locked with no snapshot is unrecoverable and is recreated.

The flush lock is the corruption signal. It is taken when the store loads and released only by a clean close. Finding it at open means the previous process did not close, so open fails and the executor restores from snapshot.

docs.title: Primitives
docs.text:
Three table shapes are built from one memory map class.

  • arraymap is positional. The link is the record index. Used for the height indexes, where the key is the height.
  • hashmap is keyed. The head is a bucket array, each bucket the link of the newest record in its chain, and each record carries the link of the next. Search hashes the key to a bucket and follows the chain. Insertion allocates the record and pushes it onto the bucket top with a compare-and-swap. A bucket also carries a small filter, derived from expected load, that rejects most misses before the chain is walked.
  • nomap is unkeyed. A slab of bytes reached only by link, used for variable-size records such as scripts.

hashmaps and nomaps are struct-of-arrays aggregates: one keyed spine plus satellite columns sharing its row count, so a record can be split into the part that is searched and the parts that are only read once found. Allocation is unified across the columns.

Records and slabs differ in their link. A record link counts rows of a fixed width. A slab link counts bytes. Link width is chosen per table and is part of the schema, so a table's maximum size is a design decision, not a runtime one.

The archive is the primary data. Everything in index and cache is derived from it and could be rebuilt. Optionals exist only if configured at creation.

The two archive hash tables that matter most are tx, keyed by tx hash, and ins, keyed by spent point. ins is how a spend is found from an outpoint, and outs is how an address is walked. Header links are three bytes, tx links four, and slab links five, which bounds the store at the sizes the schema asserts.

docs.title: Query
docs.text:
query is the only interface the node and server use. It is organized in layers, from the header comments of the class:

  • Translation. Key to link and link to link: tx hash to tx link, point to input, block to its txs and puts, output to its spenders, tx to its block.
  • Archive reads. Sizes, heights, values, fees, and the wire and object forms of headers, blocks and transactions.
  • Archive writes. Set header, set transaction, set block, and set the txs of a header, with the pruning variants that strip input scripts and witnesses.
  • Context and validation. Chain state at a header, validation state get and set, and the batching interface for captured signatures.
  • Confirmation and consensus. The strong set queries used to confirm a block, and the height indexation that maintains the candidate and confirmed chains.
  • Address, filter and unspent. The queries behind the Electrum and native address interfaces, BIP-158 filter service, and the unspent set totals and MuHash commitment.

Query holders obtain a transactor, a shared lock on the store, for the duration of an operation. Snapshot, prune and close take the exclusive side and wait for holders to drain.

docs.title: Memory management
docs.text: Heads are held in anonymous memory for the life of the load and written to file only by explicit transfer, so no dirty file-backed page exists for a head. Bodies are append only and may be staged: writes go to anonymous memory and flushed rows convert to a read-only file mapping. The consequence is that the kernel's dirty page writeback never competes with the node's own I/O, and the working set is the heads plus the tail of each body. The envelope records the bucket counts the store was created with, and bucket counts derive from installed RAM at creation, so the head set is sized to fit.
