docs.title: Developer
docs.text: The five libraries are C++20, each in its own repository, each depending only on the libraries below it. All are at version 4.0.0. This section is for building against them: which header to include, what to link, the conventions every declaration follows, and the entry points of each library.

docs.title: Including
docs.text:
Each library has one aggregate header. Include it and nothing else from that library.

Library Header Namespace Export macro system <bitcoin/system.hpp> libbitcoin::system BC_API database <bitcoin/database.hpp> libbitcoin::database BCD_API network <bitcoin/network.hpp> libbitcoin::network BCT_API node <bitcoin/node.hpp> libbitcoin::node BCN_API server <bitcoin/server.hpp> libbitcoin::server BCS_API

The aggregate headers say so themselves: API users include only this header, and direct use of other headers is fragile and unsupported. Each aggregate includes the one below it, so <bitcoin/node.hpp> brings system, database and network with it. namespace bc = libbitcoin is defined for brevity.

docs.title: Linking
docs.text:
On Linux and macOS the libraries install as libbitcoin-system, libbitcoin-database, libbitcoin-network, libbitcoin-node and libbitcoin-server, each with a pkg-config file whose Requires line chains to the libraries below it, so pkg-config --libs libbitcoin-node resolves the whole stack down to libsecp256k1 and Boost.

On Windows the libraries are not packages. Each repository's solution imports its siblings' .import.props sheets by relative path, so the five repositories are cloned side by side and built in dependency order. The property sheets define BC_STATIC or BC_DLL according to the linkage and add the sibling include and library directories.

docs.title: Conventions
docs.text:
Every declaration follows these, and code built against the libraries reads best when it does too.

  • NOEXCEPT on nearly every function. It expands to noexcept in release builds and to nothing in debug builds, so debug builds propagate assertion diagnostics. Functions that may throw, such as configuration parsing, are marked THROWS.
  • code is std::error_code in every library, and each library registers its own error category with its own error_t enumeration. Network additionally translates Boost error codes from ASIO, Beast, SSL, WebSocket, JSON and RPC into its own category.
  • cptr is std::shared_ptr<const T>, the handle for immutable values such as blocks, headers, transactions and messages. ptr is std::shared_ptr<T>, the handle for polymorphic services such as sessions, channels, protocols and the node.
  • Copy and move are declared by macro at the top of each class: DEFAULT_COPY_MOVE_DESTRUCT for value types, DELETE_COPY_MOVE_DESTRUCT or DELETE_COPY_MOVE for owners of resources or threads. The _DESTRUCT variants add a virtual defaulted destructor.
  • BC_ASSERT is a debug-only assertion. INLINE forces inlining on MSVC.
  • Handlers are moved in as rvalue references, result_handler&&, and invoked on a strand. Bind a member function with BIND, post it with POST, or run it on the pool with PARALLEL.

docs.title: Libraries
docs.text:
• system. Chain types, script machine, hashing, wallet primitives, serialization and configuration parsing.
  • database. The memory-mapped store and the query interface over it.
  • network. The proactor, sessions, channels, protocols and messages.
  • node. full_node, its configuration, the chasers and the chase event bus.
  • server. server_node, the parser, service sessions, interface declarations and dispatch.
  • Test. How the libraries are tested, and how to test code built on them.

docs.title: database
docs.text: libbitcoin-database depends on system only. It provides the store and the query interface. The Store architecture page describes the tables and their layout. This page is about using them.

docs.title: Store and query
docs.text:
The store is a template over its storage type, and the query is a template over the store.

database::settings configuration{};
configuration.path = "bitcoin";

database::store<database::mmap> store{ configuration };
database::query<database::store<database::mmap>> query{ store };

if (store.create(handler)) { /* error */ }
if (!query.initialize(genesis_block)) { /* error */ }
// ...
store.close(handler);

database::mmap is the production storage. The template parameter exists so tests can substitute an in-memory storage. The node fixes both types with the aliases node::store and node::query.

store lifecycle methods each take an event_handler called with an event and a table as work proceeds, and return a code: create from nothing, open an existing store, snapshot and prune while open, restore from snapshot while closed, reload after disk full, close. report invokes an error_handler for every table in an error or full condition. A store that is open and loaded has taken the flush and process locks. get_transactor() returns a shared lock that a query holder takes for the duration of an operation.

query is constructed over a store and is the only interface the node and server use. Its methods return bool or a value with a bool out parameter, never throw, and are thread safe against one another and against writes. It exposes the store's condition through get_fault(), is_fault(), is_full() and is_coalesced().

docs.title: Settings
docs.text: database::settings has path, the store directory, and one nested settings struct per table: simple_table for a body allocation and growth rate, bucket_table adding a bucket count, and hash_table adding an expected element count from which buckets are derived when not set. initialize(const system::settings&, bool limited) derives the defaults from the chain parameters and installed memory. Table sizing is fixed at creation and recorded in the store's envelope.

docs.title: Query surface
docs.text:
The class is large and organized in layers, each in its own implementation file under impl/query:

  • Initialization. initialize(genesis) stores the genesis block as the first candidate and confirmed block.
  • Translation. From natural keys to links and between links: to_header(hash), to_tx(hash), to_block(tx_link), to_spenders(output), to_block_txs(link) and so on. A link is the unit of identity within the store, and queries that will be followed by other queries should carry links, not hashes.
  • Archive reads. get_header, get_block, get_transaction, sizes, heights, values, fees, and the get_wire_* variants that serialize directly to a sink without constructing the object.
  • Archive writes. set(header), set(transaction), set(block) and set_txs for headers-first association, each with the context needed to store the record.
  • Validation and confirmation. Chain state at a header, validation state get and set, block_confirmable, and the height indexation that maintains the candidate and confirmed chains.
  • Address, filter and unspent. The queries behind the address interfaces, BIP-158 filters, and the unspent set totals and MuHash commitment.

Two rules from the primitives apply to anything built on the query. An accessor returned into a table body holds a shared remap lock, so use it for serialization and dispose of it immediately. Never hold an accessor into one table while reading the same table or another, or a remap waiting on your accessor while you wait on the table deadlocks. The query methods themselves respect this, so the rule bites only code that reaches below them.

docs.title: Errors
docs.text: database::code is std::error_code in the database category. The enumeration distinguishes store lifecycle errors, such as flush_lock, integrity, disk_full and mmap_failure, from table conditions. Disk full is reported as a condition, not a fault.

docs.title: network
docs.text: libbitcoin-network depends on system only. It provides the asynchronous connection layer described under Network layer and Concurrency. This page is about extending it.

docs.title: net
docs.text:
network::net(const configuration& config, const logger& log,
    uint64_t required_services, uint64_t provided_services);

start seeds and returns through its handler. run starts the inbound and outbound sessions. close blocks until the pool has joined and must not be called from a pool thread. suspend and resume stop and restart peer connections. network_settings(), service() and strand() expose the settings, the ASIO context and the strand. The thread safety contract is stated on the class: attach must be called on the network strand, and close must not be called concurrently.

docs.title: Logger
docs.text: network::logger is the log sink for the whole stack. write(level) returns a writer, a stream that commits its line when destroyed. fire(event, value) and span(event, start) record events and durations. subscribe_messages and subscribe_events receive them, which is how the executor writes files and the admin service streams. The LOGA, LOGN, LOGS, LOGP, LOGX, LOGF, LOGV and related macros write at a level and compile out when that level is not built.

docs.title: Writing a protocol
docs.text:
A protocol implements one message exchange. Derive from protocol_peer for the peer network, or from the server's HTTP and RPC protocol bases for a service.

class protocol_ping_106
  : public protocol_peer, protected tracker<protocol_ping_106>
{
public:
    typedef std::shared_ptr<protocol_ping_106> ptr;

    protocol_ping_106(const session::ptr& session,
        const channel::ptr& channel) NOEXCEPT;

    void start() NOEXCEPT override;
    void stopping(const code& ec) NOEXCEPT override;

protected:
    virtual void send_ping() NOEXCEPT;
    virtual void handle_timer(const code& ec) NOEXCEPT;
    virtual void handle_send_ping(const code& ec) NOEXCEPT;
    virtual bool handle_receive_ping(const code& ec,
        const messages::peer::ping::cptr& message) NOEXCEPT;
};

start runs on the channel strand and is where the protocol subscribes to the messages it handles with SUBSCRIBE_CHANNEL(message, handler, ...). A handler receives the code and the message and returns whether to stay subscribed. SEND(message, handler, ...) sends a message and invokes the handler on completion. SUBSCRIBE_BROADCAST and BROADCAST reach every channel's protocol of the same type, which is how a new block is announced to all peers. stopping is the place to cancel timers. A protocol can stop its channel with stop(code) but never the session or the network, and start has no failure condition.

Name a peer protocol by the protocol level that introduced its behavior, and attach it in the session according to what the peer negotiated.

docs.title: Writing a session
docs.text:
A session maintains a set of channels and supplies three things: how to make a channel from a socket, what to attach for the handshake, and what to attach afterward.

virtual channel::ptr create_channel(const socket::ptr& socket) NOEXCEPT = 0;
virtual void attach_handshake(const channel::ptr& channel,
    result_handler&& handler) NOEXCEPT = 0;
virtual void attach_protocols(const channel::ptr& channel) NOEXCEPT = 0;

start_channel runs the sequence: create, attach handshake, on success attach protocols, and subscribe to the channel's stop so the session can release it. The base provides connectors, acceptors, the stop subscription and the defer helper for retry timers. The four peer sessions and the server's session_server are the models to copy.

docs.title: Messages
docs.text:
A peer message is a struct with a cptr alias, its identifier, command string, version bounds, size(version), static deserialize and member serialize, and its fields. The message set is declared once, in interface::peer_dispatch, as a tuple of method<"command", message::cptr> entries, and messages::peer::registry derives the serializer and deserializer tables from it at compile time. Adding a message means adding the struct and one line to the tuple.

The method template is shared with the server's RPC interfaces:

template <text_t Text, typename ...Args>
struct method;

Text is the wire name, Args the parameter types with optionals last, and the constructor takes the parameter names. A notifier always injects the code as the first handler argument, so a handler for a two-parameter method takes four arguments: the code, the method tag, and the two parameters.

docs.title: Settings
docs.text: network::settings holds the peer settings, outbound, inbound and manual, the feature flags, the address pool path, and the server settings structs that client-facing services parameterize: tcp_server, secure_server, tls_server, zmtp_server, http_server and websocket_server. Each service session takes one of these as its options_t. network::configuration wraps a settings with the chain selection.

docs.title: node
docs.text: libbitcoin-node depends on database and network. It provides full_node, described under Node pipeline. This page is about embedding and extending it.

docs.title: Embedding
docs.text:
node::configuration config(chain::selection::mainnet);
// populate config.bitcoin, config.database, config.network, config.node
config.initialize();

node::store store(config.database);
node::query query(store);
store.open(handler);

network::logger log;
auto node = std::make_shared<node::full_node>(query, config, log);
node->start([&](const code& ec) { node->run(handler); });
// ...
node->close();
store.close(handler);

node::configuration composes system::settings bitcoin, database::settings database, network::settings network and node::settings node, and initialize() reads files and derives dependent settings after parsing. node::store and node::query are the aliases database::store<database::mmap> and database::query<node::store>. The node takes the query by reference and does not own the store, so the store outlives the node and is closed after it.

full_node is a network::net, so start, run, close, suspend and resume are the network's. It adds:

  • organize(header, handler) and organize(block, handler) to submit a header or block, as the peer protocols do.
  • prioritize(hash, handler), bitcoind's preciousblock.
  • submit(transactions, test, handler) to submit a package to the pool, validated only when test is set.
  • get_hashes and put_hashes, the download work interface used by the block protocols.
  • snapshot, prune and reload, each suspending the network and taking a store event handler.
  • fault(code), which suspends the network and leaves the node running.
  • archive() for the query, and accessors for each settings group.

docs.title: Chase events
docs.text:
Everything in the node coordinates through chase events. The API is on full_node:

object_key subscribe_chase(event_notifier&& handler) NOEXCEPT;
void subscribe_chase(event_notifier&& handler, event_completer&& complete) NOEXCEPT;
void unsubscribe_chase(object_key key) NOEXCEPT;
void notify(const code& ec, event_value value) NOEXCEPT;
void notify_one(object_key key, const code& ec, event_value value) NOEXCEPT;

The first subscribe_chase is for chasers and requires the node strand. The second is for protocols and completes asynchronously. An event_value is a variant of the event payloads, and to_chase(value) and to_payload<chase::x>(value) extract the event and its payload. A handler returns whether to remain subscribed. The chase enumeration documents each event's issuer and handlers, and the payload aliases height_t, header_t, object_t, count_t and transaction_t give the payload types.

docs.title: Writing a chaser
docs.text:
A chaser owns one stage of chain construction on its own strand.

class chaser_example
  : public chaser
{
public:
    chaser_example(full_node& node) NOEXCEPT;
    code start() NOEXCEPT override;
    void stopping(const code& ec) NOEXCEPT override;

protected:
    virtual bool handle_chase(const code& ec, event_value value) NOEXCEPT;
    virtual void do_something(height_t height) NOEXCEPT;
};

start is called on the node strand and is where the chaser calls subscribe_chase(BIND(handle_chase, _1, _2)) and initializes its position from the store. handle_chase runs on the notifier's strand, so it switches on to_chase(value), posts to its own strand with POST(do_something, payload), and returns. The do_ methods assert stranded() and do the work, reading and writing through archive(). To signal the rest of the pipeline, notify(error::success, chases::x{ payload }). stopping is non-blocking and stop blocks. The base provides closed(), suspended(), fault(code), resume(), and the settings accessors. Unlike a protocol, a chaser may fault the node.

full_node constructs the ten chasers as members and starts them in do_start, so adding one means adding a member and a start call. The node protocols extend network::protocol_peer and subscribe to chase events through the protocol overload, which is how block announcements and downloads are driven from the pipeline.

docs.title: Errors
docs.text: node::code is std::error_code in the node category. Its enumeration covers store lifecycle transitions such as store_snapshot and store_prune, channel dispositions such as slow_channel, stalled_channel and sacrificed_channel, and organization results such as orphan_header and duplicate_block.

docs.title: server
docs.text: libbitcoin-server depends on node. It provides server_node, the settings parser, the service sessions, the interface declarations and the bs console. This page is about adding a service or a method.

docs.title: server_node and configuration
docs.text:
server_node derives from full_node and overrides run to start the ten service sessions after the network is running. server::configuration derives from node::configuration and adds the command line state, log::settings and server::settings, which holds one settings struct per service.

server::parser derives from system::config::parser and loads four sources: command line options, positional arguments, environment variables with the BS_ prefix, and the configuration file, into parser::configured. It is constructed with the chain selection and the embedded pages of the native and admin services.

docs.title: Service sessions
docs.text:
A service is a session_server parameterized by its protocols:

template <typename ...Protocols>
class session_server
  : public server::session, public network::session_server

The first protocol supplies options_t, the settings struct the session binds with, and channel_t, the channel type it constructs. Every protocol in the list is constructed and attached to each accepted channel in order. The existing services are aliases of this template:

using session_admin = session_server<protocol_admin>;
using session_native = session_server<protocol_native>;
using session_esplora = session_server<protocol_esplora>;
using session_bitcoind = session_server<protocol_bitcoind_rest,
    protocol_bitcoind_blockchain, protocol_bitcoind_control,
    protocol_bitcoind_mining, protocol_bitcoind_network,
    protocol_bitcoind_notifications, protocol_bitcoind_test,
    protocol_bitcoind_transaction, protocol_bitcoind_utility,
    protocol_bitcoind_wallet, protocol_bitcoind>;
using session_electrum = session_handshake<protocol_electrum_version, protocol_electrum>;

protocol_bitcoind is the terminal responder for unknown methods and must be attached last. Electrum and Sparrow use session_handshake, which runs a version negotiation protocol before attaching the rest. A new service is a new alias, a new settings struct in server::settings, its options in the parser, and an attach_ and start_ pair in server_node.

docs.title: Interfaces
docs.text:
An interface declares its methods once, as a tuple of method entries, and everything else derives from that: parameter parsing, dispatch, the typed handler signatures, and the documentation on this site.

struct electrum_methods
{
    static constexpr std::tuple methods
    {
        method<"blockchain.block.header", number_t, optional<0.0>>{ "height", "cp_height" },
        method<"blockchain.transaction.get", string_t, optional<false>>{ "tx_hash", "verbose" },
        // ...
    };

    template <size_t Index> using at = method_at<methods, Index>;
    using blockchain_block_header = at<3>;
    // ...
};

Parameter types are string_t, number_t, boolean_t, value_t, object_t and array_t, with optional<default> for trailing optionals. A method declared with unimplemented is dispatchable but answered as not implemented, which keeps the interface complete while a method is pending.

docs.title: Dispatch
docs.text:
protocol_rpc<Interface> is the base for a JSON-RPC service protocol. Its start registers the interface's method names and subscribes to HTTP posts and unknown requests, and its handlers validate host and origin, check whether the method belongs to this protocol, check the credential's permission for it, and dispatch to the subscribed handler with parsed and typed arguments.

class protocol_electrum
  : public protocol_rpc<interface::electrum>
{
    using channel_t = channel_electrum;
    using options_t = channel_t::options_t;

    void start() NOEXCEPT override;

protected:
    void handle_blockchain_block_header(const code& ec,
        rpc_interface::blockchain_block_header, double height,
        double cp_height) NOEXCEPT;
};

void protocol_electrum::start() NOEXCEPT
{
    SUBSCRIBE_RPC(handle_blockchain_block_header, _1, _2, _3, _4);
    protocol_rpc::start();
}

The handler takes the code, the method tag type, and one argument per declared parameter, so the placeholder count is two plus the parameter count. Responses go through send_result, send_error, send_code and send_notification, which forward to the channel, so the same handler serves the method over raw TCP by downgrade, HTTP, and WebSocket by upgrade. A method that does not belong to any attached protocol reaches handle_unclaimed.

The bitcoind subgroups use protocol_bitcoind_dispatch<Interface> in the same way, and each subgroup is explicitly instantiated in its own translation unit so the dispatch metaprogramming compiles once.

docs.title: Adding a method
docs.text:
1. Add the method<...> entry to the interface tuple and its using alias.
  2. Declare the handler on the protocol with the code, the tag type and the typed parameters.
  3. Subscribe it in start with SUBSCRIBE_RPC.
  4. Implement it against archive(), and answer with one of the senders.
  5. Add its row to the conformance record, which regenerates the Interfaces and Conformance pages, and its acceptance test to the endpoint suite.

docs.title: system
docs.text: libbitcoin-system is the foundation library and has no libbitcoin dependency. It depends on Boost and libsecp256k1, and optionally UltrafastSecp256k1.

docs.title: Chain types
docs.text:
chain::block, chain::header, chain::transaction, chain::input, chain::output, chain::script and chain::witness are value types with the same shape. Each constructs from its parts, from a data_slice of wire bytes, from a stream, or from a reader, and each serializes with to_data. Where witness data is involved the constructor and to_data take a witness flag. Each has a cptr alias and a hash().

const chain::block block(bytes, true);
const auto hash = block.hash();
const auto wire = block.to_data(true);

Consensus checks live on the types. block::check(bool identity) performs context-free checks, and block::accept(const context&, size_t subsidy_interval, uint64_t initial_subsidy) performs those that need chain context. chain::context and chain::chain_state carry the height, timestamps, work and active fork flags at a point in the chain. chain::checkpoint and chain::compact are the supporting value types.

script::to_string(uint32_t active_flags, bool bitcoind, bool signature) renders a script, with the flags deciding how opcodes are interpreted and the bitcoind flag selecting its rendering conventions.

docs.title: Machine
docs.text: machine::interpreter evaluates scripts against a machine::program, with machine::stack and the number types implementing script numerics. This is the consensus script engine and is not normally called directly. transaction::connect invokes it per input.

docs.title: Hashing
docs.text: hash/functions.hpp provides sha256_hash, sha1_hash, sha512_hash, rmd160_hash, bitcoin_hash (double SHA-256), bitcoin_short_hash (SHA-256 then RIPEMD-160), tagged_hash for BIP-340 tagged hashes, and merkle_root. The constants null_hash, null_short_hash and one_hash are there too. The implementations dispatch at runtime to SHA-NI, AVX2, AVX-512, NEON or SVE paths where the build compiled them and the CPU supports them. hash::accumulator streams data into a hash incrementally. HMAC, HKDF, PBKDF2, scrypt, SipHash and MuHash are alongside.

docs.title: Wallet
docs.text: wallet::ec_private and wallet::ec_public wrap secp256k1 keys with WIF and hex encodings and derive wallet::payment_address, which encodes and decodes addresses and extracts the address of an output script. wallet::descriptor, the mnemonics group and the psbt group cover output descriptors, BIP-39 and Electrum mnemonics, and partially signed transactions.

docs.title: Configuration
docs.text: config::parser is the abstract base for a program's settings. A derived parser implements four loaders, for named command line options, positional arguments, environment variables under a prefix, and the configuration file, and the base merges them by precedence. The config group also holds the wrapper types that parse and serialize setting values: authorities, endpoints, hashes, paths, base encodings, blocks and scripts. system::settings holds the chain parameters, subsidy schedule, retargeting constants, genesis block and checkpoints, and system::forks is the set of consensus rule flags that a chain context activates.

docs.title: Everything else
docs.text: data and serial hold byte containers, slices and the reader and writer classes that every to_data and stream constructor uses. stream has the fast in-memory streams. endian, math and radix cover byte order, checked arithmetic and base encodings. unicode normalizes strings for mnemonics and console I/O. filter holds the Golomb-coded set for BIP-158 filters, and words the mnemonic dictionaries.

docs.title: Features
docs.text: bs is a full node and a query server in one process. It validates the chain from genesis, keeps it current from the peer network, and answers the interfaces that wallets, explorers, miners and node tooling already speak.

docs.title: One node, many interfaces
docs.text:
Each interface is a separate service with its own binding, credentials and certificates, enabled or disabled independently in configuration. Interfaces documents each method by method and Conformance tracks conformance.

Service Speaks Transport bitcoind bitcoind JSON-RPC, drop-in tcp, http, WebSocket, each with TLS bitcoind REST bitcoind REST http, https bitcoind ZMQ bitcoind ZeroMQ notifications ZMTP, CurveZMQ btcd btcd JSON-RPC, including named parameters and bitcoind methods tcp, http, WebSocket, each with TLS electrum Electrum protocol 1.0 through 1.7 with version negotiation tcp, http, WebSocket, each with TLS sparrow Electrum query interface with silent payment support advertised tcp, http, WebSocket, each with TLS esplora Esplora REST as defined by the Blockstream explorer http, WebSocket, each with TLS stratum v1 and v2 mining protocols tcp, TLS native libbitcoin's own REST and WebSocket interface, and the embedded block explorer http, WebSocket, each with TLS admin operator console: live log and event streams http, WebSocket, each with TLS peer the Bitcoin peer protocol, outbound and inbound tcp, BIP-324 encrypted transport, SOCKS5 outbound, I2P SAM inbound

The bitcoind, btcd, electrum and sparrow services accept JSON-RPC over a raw TCP socket, over HTTP, and over WebSocket on the same port, so a client's transport choice is not a server configuration decision. Native, esplora and admin objects are served as JSON, as wire bytes, or as hexadecimal text by query parameter. Full duplex services carry subscriptions: block, transaction, output and address notifications on native, header and script hash subscriptions on electrum.

docs.title: Sync
docs.text:
• Headers first. The candidate chain is built from headers and blocks are downloaded concurrently across all peers into a window of up to maximum_concurrency blocks. Slow peers are measured against their peers and split out of the work. Blocks first is available as an alternative.
  • Milestone. An operator who has validated the chain once can record a milestone. Blocks at or below it are checked for identity only, so a resync is bounded by download and storage rather than script evaluation. There is no trust assumption beyond the operator's own prior validation.
  • Full validation. Above the milestone, and from genesis if none is set, every block is checked, accepted and connected in its chain context. Signature verification is batched and, where a GPU is available, offloaded.
  • Checkpoints. Configured block hashes bound reorganization and permit identity-only checking below them.
  • Pruned. A store created pruned does not retain input scripts or witnesses under milestone or checkpoint, and advertises node_network_limited.
  • Stop height. maximum_height stops population at a height, for benchmarking and staged builds. The node idles there with the store open.

docs.title: Store
docs.text:
• Memory-mapped tables with no separate database process, write-ahead log or page cache. The operating system manages residency.
  • Fully concurrent. Writers do not block writers, readers do not block writers. Confirmation, validation and every client query run in parallel against the same store.
  • Sized to the machine. Hash table load factor derives from installed RAM at creation, so the head set fits the memory available.
  • Snapshots on a live store, with atomic directory rotation and restore after an unclean shutdown.
  • Disk full is recoverable. The node suspends the network, waits for space, and resumes without restart.
  • Optional indexes. Address index for address queries and balances. BIP-158 block and transaction filters, served to peers and clients.

docs.title: Peer network
docs.text:
• Concurrent outbound and inbound connections with black and white lists, manual peers, and a persistent address pool.
  • Protocol level negotiated per peer up to protocol_maximum, with address v2, ping nonce, reject and alert attached according to what the peer supports.
  • BIP-324 encrypted transport, selected per outbound address and advertised as node_encrypted_transport.
  • Outbound over SOCKS5 with proxy authentication, for Tor and similar. Inbound over an I2P SAM bridge.
  • Bloom filtering per BIP-37 is declined by design, and its service bit is not set.

docs.title: Operation
docs.text:
• Single executable, one optional INI configuration file, no runtime dependencies beyond the platform.
  • Console on stdin: graceful close, hot backup, suspend and resume, work report, store reload, and dumps of store sizes, records, buckets and progress.
  • Daemon on Linux with systemd readiness notification, service on Windows, launchd on macOS.
  • Logging to a two-file rotation by level, with a separate event stream, both also available live over the admin service.
  • Fee estimation over a configurable horizon of confirmed blocks, and a transaction pool with package acceptance and block templates.

docs.title: Platforms
docs.text: Linux, Windows and macOS on Intel and ARM. Hashing uses SHA-NI, AVX2 and AVX-512 on Intel and NEON and SVE on ARM, selected at runtime. Builds with GNU Autotools, CMake, and Visual Studio, compiled by g++, clang++, Xcode and Visual C++. Dependencies are Boost and libsecp256k1, plus ultrafastsecp for GPU batch verification.

docs.title: Glossary
docs.text: The vocabulary used throughout this documentation and in the code. Where a term differs from bitcoind usage the bitcoind word is given so the reader can map one to the other, but the libbitcoin word is the one that appears in identifiers, configuration and output.

docs.title: Chain
docs.text: top The highest block of a chain. bitcoind says tip. A chain is a stack, so it has a top and a bottom. top candidate, top confirmed. candidate chain The chain of headers the node currently believes to be strongest, indexed by height. Blocks on it are downloaded, validated and confirmed in order. Held in the candidate index. confirmed chain The chain of blocks that have been confirmed, indexed by height. This is the chain the node serves to clients. Held in the confirmed index. coalesced The confirmed chain has caught up to the candidate chain, so the two tops are the same header. Snapshots and the one-time prevout prune wait for this. current A chain is current when its top is within a configured window of the present time. Block download, transaction pooling and announcements start only when the chain is current. strong A transaction is strong at a height if it is in a block on the confirmed chain at or below that height. Confirmation checks that every spent output is strong and unspent. The strong_tx index records it. organize Insert a header or block into the candidate chain, reorganizing the chain if a stronger branch results. The organize chaser is the only component that changes the candidate chain. disorganize Reorganize away from a block that has failed validation or confirmation. regressed The candidate chain was reorganized to a branch point below its previous top. milestone A block hash and height the operator asserts as valid because they have validated to it before. Blocks at or below the milestone are checked for identity only. Recorded in the header at organization and fixed for the life of the store. checkpoint A block hash and height fixed in the configuration. Branches under the top reached checkpoint are rejected. Blocks under a checkpoint are checked for identity only. bypass Validation that skips script evaluation because the block is under a milestone or checkpoint. headers first Sync by organizing headers into the candidate chain and downloading their blocks concurrently. The default. The alternative, blocks first, organizes whole blocks.

docs.title: Transactions and outputs
docs.text: point A transaction hash and an output index. Identifies an output. The key of the ins table. output and input The two halves of a spend. An output holds a value and an output script. An input holds a point, an input script, a witness and a sequence. bitcoind says vout, vin, scriptPubKey and scriptSig. libbitcoin says output, input, output script, input script. prevout The output an input spends, resolved from the store. The prevout table caches them for blocks under validation. unspent set The set of outputs not yet spent by a confirmed transaction. bitcoind says UTXO set. The term appears only inside bitcoind method and field names on the wire. spender The input that spends a given output. pool The set of validated unconfirmed transactions. Open only while the chain is current. package A set of transactions submitted together and accepted or rejected as a whole. template A candidate block assembled from the pool for mining.

docs.title: Node
docs.text: chaser One stage of the node pipeline, running on its own strand. The ten chasers are header, block, check, validate, confirm, transaction, template, estimate, snapshot and storage. chase An event on the node's shared notifier. Chasers communicate only through chase events. window The span of candidate blocks currently being downloaded ahead of validation. Sized from the connection count and capped by maximum_concurrency. split Direction to a slow channel to return half its download work and stop, so a faster peer can take it. suspend and resume Stop and restart all peer connections without stopping the node. Used around snapshots, prunes and disk full. fault An unrecoverable store error. The node suspends and remains running so the operator can act. Disk full is not a fault.

docs.title: Network
docs.text: net The network object. Owns the thread pool, the strand, the hosts pool and the sessions. session Maintains a set of channels of one kind: manual, seed, inbound, outbound, or one client-server service. channel One connection, with timers and state. A channel is a proxy plus connection state. proxy The serialized message pump over a socket. Owns the read loop and the write queue. protocol One message exchange attached to a channel. Peer protocols are named by the protocol level that introduced them. level A peer protocol version number, such as 70016. hosts The pool of peer addresses learned from seeds and peers, saved to a file between runs. bind and safe A listening endpoint. A bind accepts plain connections. A safe accepts TLS connections. strand An executor that never runs two of its handlers concurrently. The unit of state ownership across the stack.

docs.title: Store
docs.text: store The set of memory-mapped tables and their lifecycle: create, open, snapshot, prune, restore, reload, close. query The interface through which the node and server read and write the store. table A head and a body. The body holds records, append only. The head holds the bucket array or the record count. head and body The two files of a table. Heads live under heads/. Bodies live at the store root. link An offset into a table body. A record link counts rows, a slab link counts bytes. Link width is fixed per table by the schema. record and slab A fixed-width row, and a variable-length byte range, in a body. bucket One cell of a hash table head, holding the link of the newest element in its chain and a filter over the chain's keys. archive, index, cache, optional The four table groups. Archive is the primary data. Index and cache derive from it. Optionals exist only if configured at creation. snapshot A copy of the heads to primary/, rotating the previous copy to secondary/. A store is restored from its snapshot after an unclean shutdown. prune Reclaim the prevout cache once the chain has coalesced. Also, for a pruned store, the stripping of input scripts and witnesses under bypass. flush lock A file held while the store is loaded and released by a clean close. Its presence at open means the store may be inconsistent and triggers a restore. envelope The settings the store was created with, recorded in the store and governing its sizing thereafter. load factor Expected elements per bucket. Derived from installed RAM at creation and fixed for the life of the store.

docs.title: Server
docs.text: service One client-facing interface on its own binding: admin, native, bitcoind, btcd, electrum, sparrow, esplora, stratum v1, stratum v2 or bitcoind zmq. bitcoind The original bitcoin node software, and the name of the service that speaks its JSON-RPC and REST interfaces. For consensus behavior the rules are satoshi's. native libbitcoin's own REST and WebSocket interface and the embedded block explorer. admin The operator's service: live log and event streams and the embedded console.

docs.title: Install
docs.text: bs is a single executable. Prebuilt binaries are not yet published, so installing means building the five libraries and the server from source. Three install scripts in the server repository do this end to end, including the dependencies, on Linux and macOS. Windows builds with Visual Studio.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text:
Requirement Version C++ compiler C++20: GCC 13 or later, Clang 16 or later, Xcode, or Visual Studio 2026 Boost 1.86.0 or later libsecp256k1 0.8.0, the bitcoin-core repository, with the ellswift, recovery and schnorrsig modules CMake 3.30 or later, for the CMake builds only Autotools autoconf, automake, libtool and pkg-config, for the GNU build only git to fetch the repositories

Optionally UltrafastSecp256k1 for GPU batch signature verification, and OpenSSL for TLS, which is on by default.

On Ubuntu 24.04:

sudo apt install build-essential git autoconf automake libtool pkg-config cmake

docs.title: Linux and macOS
docs.text: Each script clones the dependencies it is asked to build, then clones and builds libbitcoin-system, libbitcoin-database, libbitcoin-network, libbitcoin-node and libbitcoin-server in that order, runs the server tests, and installs. Repositories are cloned shallow at the master branch unless --build-full-repositories is given. Options the script does not recognize are passed through to every dependency's configure step, which is how CPU feature flags are set.

docs.title: GNU Autotools
docs.text:
git clone https://github.com/libbitcoin/libbitcoin-server
cd libbitcoin-server
./builds/gnu/install-gnu.sh --prefix=$HOME/libbitcoin --build-boost --build-secp256k1 --build-config=release --build-link=static --build-post-install-clean

The binary is $HOME/libbitcoin/bin/bs. Without --prefix it installs to /usr/local.

Option Effect --prefix=<path> Installation destination. Default /usr/local. --build-config=<mode> release or debug. --build-link=<mode> static or dynamic. --build-boost Build Boost 1.86.0 from source rather than using the system's. --build-secp256k1 Build libsecp256k1 v0.8.0 from source. --build-ultrafast Build UltrafastSecp256k1. --build-parallel=<n> Parallel jobs. Default is the hardware thread count. --build-src-dir=<path> Where sources are cloned. Default is the current directory. --build-obj-dir=<path> Intermediate objects. Default obj. --build-use-local-src Reuse sources already present instead of cloning. --build-full-repositories Full clones instead of shallow single-branch clones. --build-post-install-clean Remove dependency sources and objects after install. --build-skip-tests Do not build or run tests. --noninteractive Take defaults at every prompt. --verbose Show script output.

docs.title: CMake
docs.text:
./builds/cmake/install-cmake.sh --prefix=$HOME/libbitcoin --build-boost --build-secp256k1 --build-config=release --build-link=static

Takes the same options as the GNU script, and additionally captures -DCMAKE_PREFIX_PATH, -DCMAKE_INSTALL_PREFIX, -DCMAKE_INCLUDE_PATH and -DCMAKE_LIBRARY_PATH for the CMake configure step. libsecp256k1 is built with CMake here rather than Autotools. Feature options take the CMake form, for example -Denable-avx2=ON.

docs.title: CMake presets
docs.text:
./builds/cmake/install-presets.sh --build-preset=nix-gnu-release-static --build-boost --build-secp256k1

The preset fixes configuration and link mode, so there is no --prefix, --build-config or --build-link. Objects go to obj/<preset> and the install goes to prefix/<preset> under the source directory, so the binary is ./prefix/nix-gnu-release-static/bin/bs.

docs.title: CPU features
docs.text:
Hashing has hand-written paths for Intel SHA-NI, SSE4.1, AVX2 and AVX-512, and for ARM NEON and SVE. Which paths are compiled is a build decision. Which path runs is decided at runtime by CPUID on Intel and by the operating system's feature query on ARM, so a binary built with every path enabled runs correctly on a machine that lacks some of them.

GNU option CMake option Compiler flags --enable-shani -Denable-shani=ON -msse4 -msha --enable-sse41 -Denable-sse41=ON -msse4.1 --enable-avx2 -Denable-avx2=ON -mavx -mavx2 --enable-avx512 -Denable-avx512=ON -mavx512f -mavx512bw --with-ultrafast -Dwith-ultrafast=ON GPU batch verification

All are off by default. The ARM paths have no option and are compiled whenever the target is ARM.

docs.title: Windows
docs.text:
The solution is builds/msvc/vs2026/libbitcoin-server.sln, platform toolset v145, with StaticDebug and StaticRelease configurations for x64, Win32, ARM64 and ARM. Dependencies come from NuGet packages declared in each project's packages.config: libbitcoin-boost and its component packages at 1.91.0, secp256k1_vc145 at 0.8.0, and UltrafastSecp256k1-vc145. The sibling libbitcoin repositories are referenced by relative path through the .import.props sheets, so they must be checked out beside libbitcoin-server.

The scripted build:

.\builds\msvc\build-msvc.cmd --build-config StaticRelease --build-platform x64 --build-version vs2026 --enable-shani

Output lands under bin\<platform>\<Debug|Release>\v145\static\bs.exe. The --build-symbols option selects default, disabled or public-only debug symbols.

docs.title: Docker
docs.text:
libbitcoin-build ships a two-stage Alpine image that builds bs statically and copies only the binary and a startup script into the runtime stage. It exposes 8333 for peers and the service ports, and mounts /bitcoin/blockchain for the store and /bitcoin/conf for configuration.

docker compose --env-file bs-linux.env --file bs-linux.yml up -t 3600 -d

The long stop timeout matters. bs flushes the store on close and a SIGKILL corrupts it. Never down -v, which deletes the store volume.

docs.title: Continuous integration
docs.text: Every push builds the GNU, CMake, presets and MSVC paths across Ubuntu 24.04 with GCC 12 through 16 and Clang 18 and 19, macOS with Apple Clang, and Windows with Visual Studio 2026, in debug and release, static and dynamic. One GCC debug leg collects coverage.

All methods in the bitcoind query interface are also served here. A tcp/s transport is supported on the same port. docs.title: Operation
docs.text: bs is one executable with one optional configuration file. Started with no command it runs the node. Started with a command it performs that command and exits.

docs.title: Starting
docs.text:
bs --config bs.cfg

The configuration file path comes from --config, or from the BS_CONFIG environment variable, and is optional. Startup proceeds in a fixed order:

  1. Logging opens in the configured log directory, or on the console alone if none is set.
  2. Store. If the store directory exists it is opened. If open finds a flush lock, the previous run did not close cleanly, and the store is restored from its most recent snapshot before continuing. If the directory does not exist the store is created and the genesis block stored, so a first run needs no separate step.
  3. Reports. Body sizes, record counts, bucket counts, versions, log configuration and hardware support are written to the log.
  4. Warnings. Hardware below the compiled instruction set, memory below 8 GiB, 16 GiB or 32 GiB, disk space below 1 TiB, or a store not on an internal solid state drive each produce a warning. On a console the node then waits for Enter to continue or c to stop. --accept continues without asking.
  5. Milestone. On a fresh store without a configured milestone, the node shows the build's default milestone and asks whether to accept it as a block you have validated, or stop and set your own. Set bitcoin.milestone to the genesis hash at height zero to validate from genesis.
  6. Node. The network starts and seeds, the node runs, and the log reports that the node is started and then running.

The node runs until it is stopped. Ctrl-C, SIGINT, SIGTERM or SIGHUP, the console c command, or a service manager stop all take the same path: the network closes, the store flushes and closes, the flush lock clears, and the log ends with a shutdown line. Closing typically takes well under two minutes. On a console the process then waits for Enter before exiting.

docs.title: Commands
docs.text: Command Effect --help, -h Print the command line options. --version, -v Print the versions of the five libraries and the compiled and stored schema versions. --hardware, -w Print which instruction sets the build was compiled for and which the machine supports, and any GPU. --settings, -s Print every setting with its effective value, marking those set in configuration. --newstore, -n Create the store in the configured directory and store the genesis block. --backup, -b Snapshot the store. Works on a store that another process has open. --restore, -r Restore the store from its most recent snapshot. --daemon [true\|false], -d Install or uninstall the node as a system service. See below. --user <credential>, -u The logon account for the installed service. Default is the system account. --information, -i Print store sizes, records, buckets, collision rates and chain progress. --flags, -f Walk the candidate chain and print every consensus rule transition. --buckets, -k Print hash table bucket densities. --collisions, -l Print hash table collision distributions. Allocates heavily and may be killed on a small machine. --get <hash>, -g Run the built-in read test. --put <hash>, -p Run the built-in write test. --accept, -a Answer every startup prompt with its default.

docs.title: Console
docs.text:
While the node runs, single characters typed on the console are commands. Enter shows nothing, since echo is off.

Key Action c Close the node. Same as Ctrl-C. b Back up the store to a snapshot while running. The network is suspended for the duration and resumed after. h Hold, suspending all peer connections. g Go, resuming peer connections. Refused while the disk is full or the store is faulted. z Zeroize a disk full condition after freeing space: reload the store and resume. e Report store error conditions per table, and the bytes to free if the disk is full. i Print store configuration, body sizes, records, buckets and collision rates. w Request a work distribution report from every peer channel. t Run the built-in test case. m Print this menu.

Ten more keys toggle log levels for the running process: a application, n news, s session, p protocol, x proxy, r remote, f fault, q quitting, o objects, v verbose. A level not compiled into the build says so.

docs.title: Logs
docs.text:
Two files rotate in the log directory. bs_end.log is the current file and bs_begin.log the previous one. When the current file reaches half of log.maximum_size it becomes the previous file and a new current file starts, so the pair together never exceeds the configured size and the startup banner is gone after two rotations. Each line is a UTC timestamp, a level letter and the message. The same lines go to the console.

events.log in the same directory is not rotated. Each line is an event name, a value and the seconds since start. The events are the pipeline counters: header and block archived, validated, confirmed, organized and reorganized, bypass counts, transaction events, and timings for snapshot, prune, reload, filters and signature batches.

Both streams are also available live over the admin service.

docs.title: Running as a service
docs.text:
bs --daemon installs the node under the platform's service manager. bs --daemon false uninstalls it. Both need elevation. Starting and stopping the installed service is done with the platform's own tools. The service is installed to start automatically, with the configuration file and log directory given at install time.

  • Linux. A systemd unit at /etc/systemd/system/bs.service, type notify, wanting network-online.target, with a ten minute stop timeout. The node reports ready when running and extends the timeout while starting and stopping, so systemd never kills it mid-flush. Restart is deliberately not set.
  • Windows. A service named bs, display name Libbitcoin Server, delayed automatic start, with a ten minute pre-shutdown allowance. A non-system logon account is granted the service logon right at install.
  • macOS. A launchd daemon org.libbitcoin.bs under /Library/LaunchDaemons, run at load, output to console.log in the log directory. launchd clamps the exit timeout to sixty seconds and offers no readiness protocol.

When a Windows desktop session ends, the node blocks shutdown while it flushes, showing "Flushing tables..." as the reason.

docs.title: Store lifecycle
docs.text:
Snapshots. A snapshot copies the table heads into primary/, rotating the previous copy to secondary/, in a sequence of atomic renames. Take one from the console with b, or from a second process with bs --backup, at any time. Nothing else in the node schedules a snapshot, so a store that has never been snapshotted has no recovery path.

Unclean shutdown. Killing the process, or losing power, leaves the flush lock in place. The next start detects it and restores from primary/, or secondary/ if primary/ is incomplete, truncating the bodies to the sizes the restored heads record. Sync resumes from there. With no snapshot the store is recreated empty. Never delete the flush lock by hand. It is the only signal that the store is inconsistent.

Disk full is not a fault. The node logs the bytes required, suspends the network, fails the pending write, and checks free space every second. When space appears it reloads the store and resumes on its own. z on the console does the same on demand, and e shows how much to free.

Faults are unrecoverable store errors. The node logs the fault, suspends the network, and keeps running so the operator can inspect it with e. Snapshot and reload are refused on a faulted store. Close it and restore.

Stop height. With node.maximum_height set, the node stops requesting and validating blocks above that height and reports itself current. It does not exit. Close it as usual.

docs.title: Memory and disk
docs.text: The warning thresholds at startup state the requirements: 8 GiB of memory to run, 16 GiB for full validation, 32 GiB recommended, and 1 TiB of free disk for an unpruned mainnet store, on an internal solid state drive. The store's hash table heads are sized to the machine's RAM at creation and cannot be resized after, so create the store on the machine that will run it.

docs.title: Performance
docs.text: This section holds measured behavior of the node and the method behind the measurements. Every number here comes from a recorded run whose source state, configuration and hardware are stated beside it, and every plot is rendered from data published alongside it. Nothing is projected from a partial run.

docs.title: Measuring a sync
docs.text:
Work is proportional to transactions, not blocks. A block at height 100,000 holds a handful of transactions. A block at height 800,000 holds thousands. Half of the transactions in the first 950,000 blocks arrive after height 700,000, and the last 50,000 blocks alone carry twelve percent of them. Progress by height therefore says almost nothing about progress by work, and blocks per minute falls steeply over a sync by design, not by degradation.

Height Transactions Share 200,000 7,316,696 0.5% 400,000 112,477,764 8.3% 500,000 283,595,037 20.9% 600,000 466,297,403 34.3% 700,000 669,566,380 49.2% 800,000 868,965,224 63.9% 850,000 1,032,289,555 75.9% 900,000 1,199,374,722 88.2% 950,000 1,359,871,695 100%

Runs are normalized to height 950,000. Comparisons across machines and configurations use wall time to that height, so a run stopped earlier is compared on transactions completed, never on blocks.

Two modes, two different bottlenecks. A milestone sync does no script evaluation below the milestone, so it is paced by download, identity checks and storage, and is sensitive to network capacity, disk and the operating system's file cache. A full validation sync is paced by script evaluation and by the random reads that resolve each input's previous output against the whole archive. Its working set is the full store, so it degrades monotonically as installed RAM falls below store size and is bound by random read throughput below that point.

Peers are not a variable. The node manages peer performance aggressively, so a sync from public peers is consistent run to run. Wall time variance between identical runs is under five percent. A larger difference between two runs indicates a protocol difference between them, such as a warm cache from a preceding run, not network conditions.

A cold baseline requires a reboot. On Windows in particular, pages of a previous store or a previous run remain cached and a repeated run is always faster. Measured runs start from a reboot. Process restart alone is not cold, since mapped pages remain on the standby list.

docs.title: What governs memory
docs.text:
The hash table heads are the resident working set. Their size is the bucket count times the cell width, and bucket count is expected elements divided by load factor. At creation the load factor is derived from installed RAM so that the heads fit the memory available, with the tradeoff that a higher load factor means deeper probes during validation. That cost is paid during initial sync and is noise afterward, since a block every ten minutes does not stress probe depth. The choice is fixed for the life of the store.

Bodies are append only and are read through the operating system's file cache. Under staging, writes go to anonymous memory and completed rows convert to a read-only file mapping, so no dirty file-backed page exists and the kernel's writeback never competes with the node's own I/O.

docs.title: Recorded runs
docs.text: Measured sync times by platform, installed RAM, mode and load factor will be published here from archived run artifacts, each with its source shas, configuration and hardware. The plots follow the same rule: data file beside the figure, rendered once, never regenerated from a run in progress.

docs.title: Security
docs.text: Every service is isolated: its own listeners, its own certificates, its own credentials, its own connection and size limits. Nothing listens by default. A service exists on the network only when it has a bind and a connection limit above zero, so the attack surface of a node is exactly the set of services the operator configured.

docs.title: Listeners
docs.text:
Each service has two lists of listening addresses. bind addresses accept plain connections. safe addresses accept secured connections, TLS for the HTTP and JSON-RPC services and CurveZMQ for the ZMQ service. A service may have either, both, or neither. A safe list without the certificate and key it needs is not an error. The secured listeners are simply not created and only the plain ones serve, so check the startup log, which reports each listener as clear or private.

Bind the plain listener to loopback or a private interface, and expose only secured listeners beyond it. The peer service is the one exception. It is designed to be public and has its own controls, below.

docs.title: TLS
docs.text:
cert_path and key_path name PEM files, and key_pass decrypts the key if it is encrypted. The server context is TLS 1.2 or later. SSL 2 and 3 and TLS 1.0 and 1.1 are disabled. Cipher selection is left to the TLS library's defaults.

Client authentication is on when cert_auth names a directory of certificate authority PEM files. A client must then present a certificate that chains to one of them or the handshake fails. This is available on admin, native, bitcoind, btcd and esplora. The electrum, sparrow and stratum services offer server TLS only.

The TLS implementation is selectable at build time between OpenSSL and wolfSSL.

docs.title: Credentials
docs.text:
The bitcoind and btcd services accept HTTP basic authentication credentials of the form username:password[:method,...], repeated for as many roles as needed. A credential with a method list may call only those methods. One without may call any. The digest compared on each request is a hash of the literal authorization header value, and credentials are stored in cleartext in configuration. The settings header says what this is: compatibility for bitcoind tooling on a secured network, not security. Put TLS in front of it and scope each credential to the methods its client needs.

Authorization is latched per connection. The first request that presents a valid credential authorizes the channel for its lifetime and fixes the role that method scoping is checked against. WebSocket and raw TCP JSON-RPC frames carry no headers, so on those transports authorization is taken from the upgrade request, or for btcd from its in-band authenticate method, which every other method is refused until.

admin, native, electrum, sparrow and esplora have no credential option. Access to them is controlled by bind address, by client certificates, and for the HTTP services by host and origin checks.

docs.title: Host and origin
docs.text: The HTTP services, admin, native, bitcoind, btcd and esplora, validate the request's Host header against the host list when one is configured, and the Origin header against the origin list. A request with no origin is a same-origin request and is allowed. An opaque origin, which browsers send as null, is allowed only if allow_opaque_origin is set. A failed host check answers 400 and a failed origin check answers 403, and both close the connection. Successful responses carry access control headers reflecting the allowed origin.

docs.title: Admin and native
docs.text: These two services deserve attention because they expose the most and authenticate the least. admin streams the node's full log and event telemetry live. native serves the node's configuration and every block, transaction, output and address query the store can answer, including address histories and balances, with no history cap. Neither takes a credential. Run them on loopback, or behind mutual TLS with cert_auth, and nowhere else.

docs.title: ZMQ
docs.text: The bitcoind_zmq service secures its safe listeners with CurveZMQ. key is the server's long-term secret key in Z85. cert lists the Z85 public keys of authorized clients, and if none are listed any client holding the server's public key may connect. The handshake proves the client's long-term key through the vouch box and the server refuses unlisted keys. Every frame after the handshake is boxed with per-connection transient keys and strictly increasing nonces in each direction. A malformed key or certificate is a configuration error at startup, refused rather than silently downgraded to the unencrypted NULL mechanism, which is what the plain bind listeners always use.

docs.title: Peer network
docs.text:
• Black and white lists. network.blacklist drops the listed addresses and allows all others. network.whitelist allows only the listed addresses. Entries are addresses, addresses with ports, or CIDR subnets, and a subnet matches every address it contains. Both lists also gate connections accepted by every service.
  • Services. Peers advertising any of the service bits in peer.invalid_services are dropped. Protocol level is negotiated between peer.protocol_minimum and peer.protocol_maximum.
  • Self and loopback. inbound.self addresses are advertised to peers. Connections from the node to itself are refused unless inbound.enable_loopback is set.
  • Manual peers are maintained regardless of the address pool and excluded from pool selection.
  • Encrypted transport. BIP-324 is enabled by node.provide_privacy, which sets the node_encrypted_transport service bit. Inbound listeners then accept both v2 and v1 peers, detecting v1 and passing it through. Outbound attempts v2 only toward peers whose address record advertises the bit, so no round trip is wasted on a peer that cannot speak it.
  • Tor. Outbound and manual connections route through a SOCKS5 proxy given by outbound.socks and manual.socks, with optional username and password. Named addresses become connectable when a proxy is configured, so .onion peers can be given directly.
  • I2P. Inbound connections arrive through a SAM bridge at inbound.sam. The node's destination key is read from inbound.key_path and created there if absent, and the derived address is advertised.
  • Gossip. peer.gossip_ipv4, gossip_ipv6, gossip_tor and gossip_i2p select which address families the node relays and accepts. Only IPv4 is on by default.
  • Delayed inbound. With node.delay_inbound set, inbound peers and clients other than admin and native are refused until the chain is current.

docs.title: Limits
docs.text:
Every service carries the same limits, each configurable per service:

Limit Effect connections Channels above this count are dropped at accept without a response. Zero disables the service. rate_limit Bytes per second per channel for sending, combined with network.rate_limit by taking the more restrictive when both are set. Reads are not metered, since the protocol bounds them. maximum_request The largest request accepted. maximum_backlog The memory a channel's queued notifications may hold. A ZMQ channel over its backlog drops the message, since ZMQ messages are sequenced. Any other channel over its backlog is stopped as congested. Each queued message is charged a fixed overhead so a flood of tiny messages cannot evade the bound. inactivity_minutes A channel with no traffic for this long is closed. expiration_minutes A channel is closed after this long regardless of traffic. connect_timeout_seconds Connection establishment limit, falling back to the network setting and randomized between half and full to spread retries.

Responses are never queued against the backlog. Only notifications are, so a client cannot exhaust the node by subscribing and not reading.

docs.title: Secrets in output
docs.text: bs --settings prints every setting with its value, except those declared secret, which print empty and disclose only that they are set: private key passwords, service credentials, SOCKS5 passwords and the ZMQ server key.

docs.title: Test
docs.text:
How the stack is tested, at every level from a single method to a synced node on the public network. Each method answers a different question and none substitutes for another.

Level Question Where Unit Does this method do what its contract says, with its callees faked? test/ in each library Component Do several units compose, such as connect with the interpreter unmocked? test/ in each library Protocol fixture Does a service dispatch each method and shape its response? libbitcoin-server/test/protocols/ Acceptance Does a real client get the right answer from a live, synced node? libbitcoin-server/endpoints/ Conformance Does each interface method match the protocol? the conformance record behind Conformance Sync Does the node validate the chain and how fast, from genesis, from public peers? Performance Coverage Which lines no test reaches? CI and local measurement

docs.title: Unit tests
docs.text:
Every library has one Boost.Test binary under test/, mirroring the src/ and include/ tree one test file per source file.

Library Cases system 6,411 database 1,104 network 1,600 server 1,176 node 115

Unit tests are built and run in release configuration, since that is what ships, and are run on every push across every compiler and platform in the CI matrix. Debug builds are used only to debug.

A test is one method under one condition with one expected result, and its name says so: subject__method__condition__result, with the result being the error code where one applies.

BOOST_AUTO_TEST_CASE(block__constructor__data__expected)
BOOST_AUTO_TEST_CASE(hashmap__slab_construct__non_empty__expected_enabled)

Style rules. No loops and no conditions in a test body or a fixture. A small range is written out as explicit assertions with numbered locals. Every assertion stays on one line however long, with nested expressions hoisted into named locals rather than wrapped. Comment almost nothing, since the name and the code are the documentation. Helpers are static free functions. Vocabulary is libbitcoin's, not bitcoind's.

Property tests and reference tests, both. A round-trip test, serialize then deserialize, proves consistency. A property test, member matches and non-member does not, proves shape. Neither proves correctness, since both pass against an implementation that is consistently wrong. So every encoding and every consensus rule also has a reference test pinning exact published bytes: BIP test vectors for scripts, transactions, witnesses, taproot, addresses, keys, mnemonics and descriptors, NIST vectors for the hash functions, and libbitcoin's own vectors captured from the chain. The system tests reference the relevant BIP by number at each such assertion, which is how a reader finds the source of the expected value.

Unit coverage independent of component coverage. A unit test fakes what the method calls, so that its lines are covered by its own tests and not incidentally by a component test above it. Mock seams are explicit: the machine tests use an accessor exposing the interpreter's protected surface, the database tests substitute an in-memory storage for the memory map so no files are touched, the network tests use mock sockets, acceptors, connectors and channels with scripted success and failure, and the node tests mock the network and query.

Unreachable guards become assertions, not exclusions. A branch that cannot be reached is converted to BC_ASSERT rather than excluded from coverage, since excluding it would hide a defect if it ever became reachable.

docs.title: Protocol fixtures
docs.text: Each server interface has a fixture under test/protocols/<interface>/ that constructs a server_node over a small mocked store and attaches the service's session, so a test can send a request through the real dispatch path and assert on the response object. These tests prove that every declared method dispatches, parses its parameters, and serializes its result. They run in the unit test binary and need no network.

docs.title: Acceptance
docs.text:
libbitcoin-server/endpoints/ is a pytest suite of real clients against a live node over real sockets: requests for HTTP, websocket-client for WebSocket, raw sockets for Electrum, and a standard-library WebSocket client for btcd. One file per interface, plus a transports file that exercises the same methods over TCP, HTTP and WebSocket to prove the transport does not change the answer.

The node under test is synced against the public network to at least height 500,000 so that every test applies, including witness cases from height 481,824. Expected values are reference blocks and transactions from the chain, so a wrong answer is a wrong answer, not a disagreement with a mock.

An interface is not done until it has its file here. The fixture proves dispatch and shape. The acceptance suite proves the answer.

docs.title: Conformance
docs.text: For the bitcoind, btcd, Electrum and Esplora interfaces, conformance is to the protocol, and the conformance record marks each method Full, Partial, Pending, WIP, Rejected or Scope with a note. Full means the method behaves as the protocol specifies on the same input, including error codes and the JSON types of every field. Number serialization form is not a difference. Value and type are. Rejected methods carry the reason, which is usually a privacy leak or a mining or wallet responsibility the node does not take on. The record is the single source for the landing page and for the Conformance and Interfaces sections.

docs.title: Sync
docs.text:
A full synchronization from genesis against public peers is the end-to-end test of the node: every block validated, every rule exercised in chain context, every peer protocol driven by real peers. It is also the benchmark. Performance states the method: work measured in transactions not blocks, runs normalized to height 950,000, a cold start from reboot, a pinned source state recorded with every run, and run artifacts archived before the next run overwrites them. A run from an uncommitted tree supports no conclusion.

Milestone sync tests the pipeline without script evaluation. Full validation tests everything. A run that stops at a configured height with maximum_height tests a bounded portion, and a store snapshot taken at that height is the starting point for the next.

docs.title: Coverage
docs.text:
CI builds one leg with GCC in debug configuration and --coverage, runs the tests, and uploads line coverage to Coveralls, excluding the test tree, the examples, the bundled QR encoder and the mnemonic word catalogs. The exclusions are declared once in libbitcoin-build and generated into every repository's workflow.

Locally on Windows the same measurement comes from the code coverage console shipped with Visual Studio, instrumenting the debug test binary through its PDB. Two rules make the numbers honest. Measure the debug build, since optimization reattributes lines to call sites and folds others away. And take the maximum over instantiations per source line, since a template line appears once per instantiation and is covered if any of them ran. Coverage is a map of what no test reaches, and the test written to reach a line must still assert a reference value, or it merely records what the code does.

docs.title: Continuous integration
docs.text: Every push to every repository builds and tests the GNU Autotools, CMake and CMake presets paths on Ubuntu with GCC 12 through 16 and Clang 18 and 19, macOS with Apple Clang, and Windows with Visual Studio 2026, in debug and release and static and dynamic linkage. The workflows are generated from libbitcoin-build, so the matrix is the same shape in every repository and a change to it lands everywhere at once. The install scripts run the server's tests at the end of every scripted build unless told not to.
